extracted.intended_audience: potential opponents and patent proprietors (and their patent attorneys) considering or engaged in European Patent Office opposition proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for filing, prosecuting, and defending oppositions against granted European patents before the EPO, including admissibility, grounds, procedure, timing, costs and likely outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central revocation via opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppositions are the only way that a European patent can be revoked centrally during a limited period after grant; after the opposition period, revocation must be sought nationally in each state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions can be lengthy but are generally far less expensive and time consuming than multiple national revocation proceedings. Use opposition where central revocation is desired within the allowable time window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for filing
rubrics_metrics.description: An opposition must be filed within nine months of the official date of grant of the European patent, and the opposition fee must be paid by the same date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No extensions are possible to the nine‑month deadline and the EPO ten‑day postal rule does not apply. Missing the deadline renders opposition inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be opponent
rubrics_metrics.description: Any natural or legal person (other than the owner of the patent being opposed) may file an opposition; more than one opposition may be filed and opponents may act jointly or separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A firm of patent attorneys may file in their own name to conceal the opponent's identity. Opposition status cannot easily be transferred—legal persons can transfer/assign an opposition only together with the business assets in the interests of which the opposition was filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required statement of grounds and early substantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: An opposition must include a statement of the grounds on which the patent is opposed; there are limited permitted grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When opposing, set out as full a case as possible at the outset with all relevant facts, evidence and arguments. If a ground of opposition is not mentioned and substantiated initially, it may not be possible to introduce it later during the proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted grounds for opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The grounds are limited and include: (1) that the subject‑matter is not patentable (lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, lacking industrial application or excluded subject‑matter); (2) that the invention is not sufficiently described to allow a person skilled in the art to carry it out (insufficiency); and (3) that the subject‑matter extends beyond the content of the application as filed (added matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions must identify which of these grounds are relied upon and provide supporting evidence/arguments. Grounds outside these categories are generally not admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Before substantive examination, the opposition division examines whether the opposition has been validly filed (admissible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common admissibility issues include non‑payment of the fee on time or failure to unambiguously identify the opponent. Inadmissible oppositions are rejected without substantive examination; such rejections are appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and role of the opposition division
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition proceedings are conducted before an opposition division comprising three technically qualified examiners (at least two of whom must not have taken part in grant), and sometimes a legally qualified examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPO acts as the judge, assessing inter partes arguments. Expect technically qualified assessors; ensure technical and legal arguments are presented appropriately for such a panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural format and oral proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings are initially conducted by written correspondence and will end in an oral hearing only if one is requested by a party during the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent proprietors and interested parties (and their attorneys) may attend oral proceedings but attendance is not compulsory. Typical sequence: admissibility check → proprietor invited to file observations → optional rounds of comments → request for hearing triggers summons → final written submissions → oral proceedings (if held) → written decision. Timings between steps are typically measured in months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition proceedings are contentious and inter partes, making outcomes hard to predict and creating uncertainty regarding patent validity until decision is issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions often take over two years to conclude; if an appeal is filed by an adversely affected party the uncertainty can extend for a further two years or more. Plan infringement/portfolio strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible outcomes and limitation on scope of amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical outcomes are revocation, maintenance in amended (limited) form, or maintenance as granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately one third of opposed patents are revoked, one third maintained in amended form (patent scope cannot be broadened after grant), and one third maintained as granted. When defending, prepare fall‑back amendment positions because broadening is not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost drivers and typical cost ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs depend on length/complexity of the patent, number of claims, number of documents to analyse, and how much of the work is done by the representative versus being provided by the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical opponent/proprietor cost examples given: preparing and filing notice of opposition £2,000–£10,000 (≈£4,000 typical); reviewing proprietor’s observations £1,000–£3,000 (~£1,000 typical); further observations £0–£5,000 (~£2,000 typical); preparing for oral proceedings £1,000–£5,000 (~£3,000 typical); attending oral proceedings £3,000–£10,000 (~£4,000 typical). Overall typical total ~£10,000–£35,000 (typical £15,000–£20,000) over 2–3 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who bears costs; apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: To a large extent each side must bear its own costs in an opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment of costs may be made by the opposition division only in certain limited circumstances (e.g. abuse of procedure) and only if requested before the final decision is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: National renewal fees continue
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual renewal fees are still payable on the individual granted national patents during an opposition process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget to keep paying national renewal fees while an opposition is pending; non‑payment can affect national rights independent of the opposition outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and implementation of amendments after opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent is amended as a result of an opposition, a procedure similar to that following a notice of allowance before grant is followed to implement the amendments in each designated state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments accepted at the EPO must still be implemented at national level by following the relevant post‑grant national procedures; expect additional administrative work and possibly fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical timeline expectations for procedure steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical delays between key events are indicated (e.g. +6–9 months to proprietor observations after filing; further +6–9 months to further observations; +4–6 months to summons for oral proceedings; +1–4 months to written decision after oral proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the flowchart timings as a simplified guide for planning resources and client expectations; individual cases may vary significantly.
